mainTopic: A stolen סוכה and stolen building materials; whether a dry לולב or אתרוג is kosher, and the rule of הדר
overview: This amud opens by finishing an earlier question about a myrtle: even an uncut myrtle is sometimes called הושענא, so cutting it is not a real change of name. Then a ברייתא records that רבי אליעזר disqualifies a stolen סוכה and a סוכה built in רשות הרבים, while חכמים allow them. רב נחמן explains that the argument is about someone who forcibly takes over another person's סוכה. If someone only stole wood and used it as סכך, everyone agrees the owner gets just the value of the wood. A story follows: An old woman complains that her wood went into the ריש גלותא's סוכה, and רב נחמן tells the scholars that she is owed only its value. רבינא adds that a stolen beam in a סוכה is also paid back with money during the חג, under תקנת מריש. The גמרא then turns to a dry לולב. רבא says the argument depends on whether the לולב is compared to the אתרוג for הדר. The גמרא defends רבא against challenges about tying the לולב, then challenges his claim about the אתרוג with a ברייתא where רבי יהודה allows dry species. רבי יהודה's supporting story continues on the next amud.

steps.title: A myrtle is called הושענא even before it is cut
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes the challenge (the myrtle's name changed to הושענא) and answers that even before cutting, people sometimes call a myrtle הושענא, so there is no real change of name.
steps.simpleTranslation: [The challenge ended:] '...and now it is called a הושענא!' The answer: even from the start, people also call a myrtle 'הושענא.'
steps.whatsHappening: The first word finishes a question from just before: a cut myrtle gets a new name, הושענא, so maybe that change of name lets the person who cut it acquire it. The גמרא answers that the name is not really new.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A real שינוי השם (change of name) can help a person acquire something that came to him wrongly. Here, though, the name הושענא is sometimes used for a myrtle that is still growing. So cutting it does not create a new name, and it does not count as a change.

keyTerms.meaning: A name for the branches used on סוכות, here especially the myrtle
A change of name, which can count as a real change in the object

steps.confusionAlert: The word הושענא at the very start is not a new statement. It is the last word of the question from before the answer.

phrases.english: a hoshana!
phrases.notes: This finishes the earlier question: before it was called a myrtle, and now it's called a hoshana!

phrases.english: Originally, too,
they call a myrtle 'hoshana.'

steps.triggerLanguage: מֵעִיקָּרָא, נָמֵי לְאַסָּא הוֹשַׁעְנָא קָרוּ לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from the previous daf that cutting the myrtle changes its name
steps.terutzResolutionType: Denies the premise: the name was never really changed
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Cutting the myrtle changes its name to הושענא, so the cutter acquires it through שינוי השם
steps.terutzMaskana: Since a myrtle is sometimes called הושענא even before cutting, there is no change of name

steps.title: Stolen סוכה and סוכה in רשות הרבים: the dispute
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא: רבי אליעזר disqualifies a stolen סוכה and a סוכה covered with סכך in רשות הרבים; חכמים say they are kosher.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: a stolen סוכה, and one who puts סכך on a סוכה in the public domain: רבי אליעזר disqualifies, and the חכמים declare it kosher.
steps.whatsHappening: A new topic begins. The גמרא quotes a ברייתא in which רבי אליעזר and חכמים argue whether a stolen סוכה, or one built on public land, can be used for the מצוה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Building in רשות הרבים is like taking land that belongs to the public, so both cases involve some form of stealing. רבי אליעזר says such a סוכה is פסול, and חכמים say it is כשר. The ברייתא does not say what kind of stealing it means; the next step will explain that.

keyTerms.meaning: One who puts on the סכך (the roof covering)

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
A stolen sukkah,
and one who puts on schach in the public domain —
Rabbi Eliezer disqualifies,
and the Sages declare it kosher.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic after the myrtle discussion ends
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי אליעזר: a stolen סוכה or one in רשות הרבים is פסול; חכמים: כשר

steps.title: רב נחמן: the dispute is about taking over someone's סוכה
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן limits the dispute to a case where someone overpowers his friend and forces him out of his סוכה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said: The dispute is where one overpowers his fellow and pushes him out of his סוכה.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן explains exactly which case the ברייתא means by a 'stolen סוכה': someone forcibly took over another person's finished סוכה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The case is not someone who stole wood and built a סוכה. The robber grabbed a סוכה that was already standing on the owner's land. This setup allows the next steps to explain both sides by their known opinions.

phrases.english: Rav Nachman said:
The dispute is where one overpowers his fellow
and pushed him out of his sukkah.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן: מַחְלוֹקֶת בְּשֶׁתּוֹקֵף אֶת חֲבֵירוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defines the case of 'stolen סוכה' in the ברייתא
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The dispute is about forcibly taking over another person's סוכה

steps.title: רבי אליעזר's reasoning: it is not his own סוכה either way
steps.stepSummary: רבי אליעזר holds that one cannot fulfill the מצוה in another person's סוכה. So whether land can be stolen (a stolen סוכה) or not (a borrowed סוכה), the robber does not fulfill his obligation.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי אליעזר follows his own reasoning, since he said a person does not fulfill his obligation in his friend's סוכה. If land can be stolen, it is a stolen סוכה. And even if land cannot be stolen, it is a borrowed סוכה.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן explains why רבי אליעזר disqualifies the סוכה: it follows from his opinion elsewhere that you need your own סוכה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two options. If land can be stolen, the robber owns it through theft, and it is a stolen סוכה. If land cannot be stolen, it still belongs to the owner, so the robber is only using someone else's סוכה, like a borrowed one. Either way, for רבי אליעזר it is not the robber's own kosher סוכה.

keyTerms.meaning: Land can be stolen (legally taken by a robber)

phrases.english: And Rabbi Eliezer follows his own reasoning,

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר: אֵין אָדָם יוֹצֵא יְדֵי חוֹבָתוֹ
phrases.english: as he said: A person does not fulfill his obligation
in the sukkah of his fellow.
If land can be stolen —
it is a stolen sukkah.
And even if land cannot be stolen —
it is a borrowed sukkah.
phrases.notes: Either way it isn't really his own סוכה, so according to רבי אליעזר he can't use it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the reason for רבי אליעזר's ruling in the case רב נחמן defined
steps.mimraCoreRuling: For רבי אליעזר, the robber fails either way: the סוכה is either stolen or borrowed, and you cannot use another person's סוכה

steps.title: חכמים's reasoning: land cannot be stolen, so it is just borrowed
steps.stepSummary: חכמים hold that one can fulfill the מצוה in another person's סוכה, and that land cannot be stolen. So the סוכה is only 'borrowed,' and the robber fulfills his obligation.
steps.simpleTranslation: And חכמים follow their own reasoning, since they said a person fulfills his obligation in his friend's סוכה. Land cannot be stolen, so the סוכה counts as a borrowed one.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן explains why חכמים call the סוכה kosher: it follows from two of their opinions.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since land cannot be stolen, the סוכה still belongs to the owner, so it is not a 'stolen סוכה.' The robber is only using someone else's סוכה, and for חכמים that is fine. So the robber fulfills the מצוה, even though what he did was wrong.

keyTerms.meaning: Land cannot be stolen; it always stays with its true owner

steps.whatToRemember: According to רב נחמן, the dispute about a stolen סוכה depends on two questions: can you use someone else's סוכה, and can land be stolen? רבי אליעזר: the robber fails either way. חכמים: land cannot be stolen, so it is a borrowed סוכה, and that works.
steps.confusionAlert: חכמים are not saying that taking over the סוכה was allowed. They only say that the robber still fulfills the מצוה, because legally the סוכה is borrowed, not stolen.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows how one ruling can grow out of two separate principles: using another person's סוכה, and whether land can be stolen.

phrases.english: And the Rabbis follow their own reasoning, as they said:
A person fulfills his obligation
in the sukkah of his fellow,
and land cannot be stolen,
so it is a borrowed sukkah.
phrases.notes: Since the land never stopped being the owner's, the robber is just using someone else's סוכה, which חכמים allow.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the other side of רב נחמן's explanation, matching the explanation of רבי אליעזר
steps.mimraCoreRuling: For חכמים, land cannot be stolen, so the סוכה is borrowed, and one can fulfill the מצוה in another person's סוכה

steps.title: Stolen wood used as סכך: everyone agrees the owner gets only its value
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן finishes his limitation. If someone stole wood and used it as סכך, both רבי אליעזר and חכמים agree that the owner is owed only the value of the wood.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if he stole wood and covered a סוכה with it, everyone agrees that the owner has a claim only to the value of the wood.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן finishes his point. The argument between רבי אליעזר and חכמים is only about taking over someone else's סוכה, not about stealing wood to build one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With stolen wood, the owner can only demand payment, so the סוכה counts as the robber's own. That is why even רבי אליעזר agrees here. The real argument is only about grabbing the land and the whole סוכה from someone else.

keyTerms.meaning: he covered the סוכה with סכך (the roof)
the money value of the wood

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up a 'stolen סוכה' with a 'סוכה made of stolen wood.' The argument in the ברייתא is only about the first. In the second, everyone agrees the סוכה is fine and the owner just gets paid.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the basic rule behind the story later on. Stolen building materials only create a debt of money; they do not make the סוכה stolen.

phrases.english: But if he stole wood and covered [a סוכה] with it —
everyone agrees
he [the owner] has only [a claim to] the value of the wood.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes רב נחמן's limitation from Step 3 by naming the case that is NOT part of the argument.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Stolen wood used as סכך: everyone agrees the owner gets only the value of the wood, and the סוכה is valid.

steps.title: How does רב נחמן know this?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks where רב נחמן gets the idea that the ברייתא is talking about taking over a סוכה and not about stolen wood.
steps.simpleTranslation: From where [do we know this]?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for רב נחמן's source. This short question sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא just says 'a stolen סוכה,' which could also mean a סוכה built from stolen materials. The גמרא wants to know what in the ברייתא shows it means taking over the land.

phrases.english: From where [do we know this]?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source of רב נחמן's limitation in Steps 3 and 6.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What in the ברייתא shows that 'stolen סוכה' means taking over the land and not stealing the wood?

steps.title: The ברייתא pairs a stolen סוכה with a סוכה in public space
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא puts a stolen סוכה next to a סוכה in רשות הרבים. Just as public land is not his, the stolen סוכה is also about land that is not his.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because the ברייתא teaches it alongside רשות הרבים. Just as in רשות הרבים the land is not his, so too with the stolen סוכה, the land is not his.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question. The proof comes from which case the ברייתא placed right next to the stolen סוכה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since both cases appear together, they share one problem. The only problem with a סוכה in רשות הרבים is that the ground does not belong to him. So the stolen סוכה must also be a case of land that is not his, meaning he took over someone's סוכה, and not a case of stolen wood.
steps.whatToRemember: The stolen סוכה in the ברייתא is about the LAND not being his, just like a סוכה in public space. It is not about stolen building materials.

phrases.english: Since it teaches [it] alongside [a סוכה in] public space.
phrases.notes: The ברייתא from Step 2 listed both cases together: the stolen סוכה and the סוכה in public space.

phrases.english: Just as [with] public space —
the land is not his,
so too [the stolen] סוכה —
it is land that is not his.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 7 by reading the structure of the ברייתא from Step 2.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Because the ברייתא pairs it with a סוכה in public space, where the only problem is the land, the stolen סוכה must also be about land that is not his.

steps.title: An old woman complains that the ריש גלותא used her stolen wood
steps.stepSummary: An old woman comes to רב נחמן and says the ריש גלותא and his scholars are sitting in a סוכה built from what was taken from her. When he ignores her, she protests that a daughter of אברהם אבינו deserves attention.
steps.simpleTranslation: A certain old woman came before רב נחמן and said: The ריש גלותא and all the scholars of his house are sitting in a stolen סוכה. She screamed, but רב נחמן paid no attention. She said: A woman whose father had 318 servants is screaming before you, and you pay no attention to her?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story that puts the rule about stolen wood into practice. This part only sets up the case; רב נחמן's ruling comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: She calls it a 'stolen סוכה,' but really what was taken was her wood. That is exactly the case from Step 6. Her protest about her father's 318 servants is her demand to be treated with respect as a descendant of אברהם.

keyTerms.meaning: the head of the Jewish community in exile (the Exilarch)

phrases.aramaic: הָהִיא סָבְתָּא דַּאֲתַאי לְקַמֵּיהּ דְּרַב נַחְמָן,
phrases.english: A certain old woman who came before רב נחמן,
said to him:

phrases.aramaic: רֵישׁ גָּלוּתָא וְכוּלְּהוּ רַבָּנַן דְּבֵי רֵישׁ גָּלוּתָא
phrases.english: The ריש גלותא and all the scholars of the ריש גלותא's house
are sitting in a stolen סוכה.

phrases.aramaic: צָוְוחָה וְלָא אַשְׁגַּח בָּהּ רַב נַחְמָן.
phrases.english: She screamed, and רב נחמן paid no attention to her.
She said to him:
A woman whose father had
phrases.notes: She means אברהם אבינו, the father of every Jew. See בראשית 14:14.

phrases.english: three hundred and eighteen servants
is screaming before you, and you pay no attention to her?!

steps.triggerLanguage: הָהִיא סָבְתָּא דַּאֲתַאי לְקַמֵּיהּ דְּרַב נַחְמָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a real-life case that matches the stolen-wood rule from Step 6.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Setup: a complaint that the ריש גלותא's סוכה was built with materials taken from the woman.

steps.title: רב נחמן rules she gets only the value of the wood
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן tells the scholars that the woman is just a screamer, and that she is owed only the money value of her wood.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said to them: This one is a screamer, and she has a claim only to the value of the wood.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן gives his ruling in the story. He applies the rule from Step 6: when wood is stolen, the owner only gets paid back for it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because only wood was taken, and not land or a whole סוכה, she cannot demand her wood back or call the סוכה invalid. The ריש גלותא's סוכה stays kosher, and she gets money for the wood.
steps.whatToRemember: A סוכה built from stolen wood is still kosher, because the owner only gets the value of the wood. Only taking over someone's whole סוכה is what רבי אליעזר and חכמים argue about.

phrases.english: רב נחמן said to them:
phrases.notes: 'Them' is the scholars around him, not the woman.

phrases.english: This one is a screamer,

phrases.aramaic: וְאֵין לָהּ אֶלָּא דְּמֵי עֵצִים בִּלְבַד.
phrases.english: and she has only [a claim to] the value of the wood.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לְהוּ רַב נַחְמָן: פָּעִיתָא הִיא דָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the story from Step 9 by applying the rule from Step 6.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Stolen wood used as סכך leaves the owner with only a claim for its value. The סוכה remains valid.

steps.title: A stolen beam in a סוכה is also paid back with money
steps.stepSummary: רבינא rules that a stolen beam used in a סוכה falls under the Rabbis' enactment: the thief pays its value instead of taking apart the סוכה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said: For a stolen beam used in a סוכה, the Rabbis made a special enactment, based on the enactment about a stolen beam built into a house.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא adds a new ruling. Even a big beam that was stolen and built into a סוכה is paid back with money, not returned.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally a thief must return the exact item he stole. The Rabbis made an exception for a beam built into a building, so the thief would not have to tear it down. רבינא applies that same exception to a beam in a סוכה.

keyTerms.meaning: A rabbinic enactment or special rule
The Rabbis' rule that a stolen beam built into a building is paid back with money

steps.whyThisMatters: It extends the earlier ruling about stolen wood, from step 10, to a bigger and rarer item.

phrases.english: Ravina said:
This beam of a sukkah that is stolen,
the Rabbis made an enactment for it,
because of the enactment of the beam.
phrases.notes: This is the known rule that if someone builds a stolen beam into a building, he can pay for it instead of tearing the building down.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Extends רב נחמן's ruling about stolen wood to a stolen beam.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A stolen beam in a סוכה is paid back with money because of תקנת מריש.

steps.title: Why say this? It seems obvious
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רבינא needed to say this, since a beam seems no different from the wood already discussed.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is obvious! How is a beam different from wood?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבינא: we already know stolen wood is paid back with money, so why should a beam be any different?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge is that רבינא's statement looks unnecessary. If the rule works for wood, a beam is just more wood, so what new thing is he teaching?

keyTerms.meaning: It is obvious, so why say it?

phrases.english: It is obvious!
How is it different from wood?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges whether רבינא's ruling adds anything new.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A beam is just wood, and the wood ruling is already known, so the statement looks unnecessary.

steps.title: A beam is rare, so we might have thought it must be returned
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that wood is common, but a big beam is rare, so we might have thought the owner wants it back. רבינא teaches that the rule still applies.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have said: wood is common, but this beam is not common, so the enactment should not apply. So רבינא teaches us that it does.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the new point in רבינא's ruling. Since a large beam is hard to find, we might have thought the thief must give back the real beam.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Wood is easy to replace, so paying money seems fair. A large beam is rare, so maybe the owner would insist on getting it back. רבינא teaches that even so, money is enough.

keyTerms.meaning: You might have said (a mistaken first thought)

phrases.english: You might have said: wood is common,
but this one is not common —
so say no,
phrases.notes: Meaning: say the money rule does not apply, and he must give back the actual beam.

phrases.english: so he teaches us.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the פשיטא challenge.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Shows the statement is needed to block a reasonable mistake
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A rare beam must be returned, because it is hard to replace.
steps.terutzMaskana: Even a rare beam falls under the enactment and is paid back with money.
steps.whatToRemember: Even a rare, large beam in a סוכה is paid back with money, just like ordinary wood.

steps.title: The rule applies only during the seven days, unless the beam was cemented in
steps.stepSummary: The money rule applies only during סוכות. After the חג the beam goes back to the owner, unless it was fixed in place with mortar.
steps.simpleTranslation: This applies only during the seven days. After the seven days, the beam goes back as is. But if he attached it with mortar, even after the seven days he just pays its value.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sets a time limit on the rule. During סוכות the thief pays money, but after the חג he must return the actual beam, unless he attached it permanently with mortar.
steps.deeperAnalysis: During the חג, taking the סוכה apart would be a big loss, so the Rabbis let him pay. After the חג, the סוכה is no longer needed, so he can easily return the beam. If it was cemented in, it is like a permanent building, so the money rule stays.

keyTerms.meaning: These words apply (only in this case)
Within the seven days of סוכות
Goes back in its original form

steps.confusionAlert: The beam does not stop belonging under the enactment for no reason after the חג. The point is that after סוכות there is no more need to keep it in the סוכה, so he can return it, unless it is cemented in permanently.

phrases.english: This applies within the seven days,
but after the seven days
it goes back as it is.
And if he attached it with mortar,
then even after the seven days too
he gives him the money.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits רבינא's ruling to the days of the חג, with an exception for a cemented beam.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Money is paid during the חג; after the חג the beam is returned, unless it was attached with mortar.
steps.whatToRemember: Stolen beam in a סוכה: during the חג, pay money. After the חג, return the beam. If cemented in, pay money even after the חג.

steps.title: A ברייתא: a dry one is unfit, but רבי יהודה says it is fit
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens a new topic with a ברייתא: a dry one is unfit, and רבי יהודה disagrees.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught: A dry one is unfit. רבי יהודה says it is fit.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא leaves the stolen סוכה topic and brings a ברייתא about a dry item used for the מצוה. This sets up רבא's explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא records an argument but does not say exactly what item it means, or why they argue. רבא will explain both points next.

keyTerms.meaning: Unfit, cannot be used for the מצוה

phrases.english: It was taught:
A dry one is unfit,
Rabbi Yehuda rules it fit.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic, moving from the stolen סוכה to a dry לולב.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: חכמים rule a dry one unfit; רבי יהודה rules it fit.

steps.title: רבא: the argument is only about a לולב, not an אתרוג
steps.stepSummary: רבא explains that the argument is only about a לולב. חכמים compare it to an אתרוג, which must be beautiful. רבי יהודה does not compare them. For an אתרוג, everyone agrees it must be beautiful.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: The argument is about a לולב. חכמים hold that we compare a לולב to an אתרוג: just as an אתרוג must be beautiful, so too a לולב must be beautiful. רבי יהודה holds that we do not compare a לולב to an אתרוג. But for an אתרוג, everyone agrees it must be beautiful.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא explains the ברייתא from step 15. He says what the argument is about, and he explains the reason behind each side.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק requires an אתרוג to be הדר, beautiful, and a dry one is not beautiful. חכמים apply that same requirement to the לולב because they are listed together, so a dry לולב is unfit. רבי יהודה does not compare them, so for him a dry לולב is fit. Still, a dry אתרוג is unfit according to everyone.

keyTerms.meaning: We compare (learn one item from another listed next to it)
Beautiful, from the פסוק 'פרי עץ הדר'

steps.whatToRemember: Dry אתרוג: unfit according to everyone. Dry לולב: unfit according to חכמים, who compare it to the אתרוג; fit according to רבי יהודה, who does not.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the whole argument depends on one question: do we compare the לולב to the אתרוג for the rule of הדר?

phrases.english: Rava said: The dispute is about a lulav,
for the Rabbis hold:
we compare the lulav to the etrog,
phrases.notes: They are compared because both appear in the same פסוק, ויקרא 23:40.

phrases.english: just as an etrog needs "beauty,"
so too a lulav needs "beauty."
And Rabbi Yehuda holds:
we do not compare the lulav to the etrog.
But regarding an etrog —
everyone agrees we need beauty.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains what the ברייתא's argument is about and the reasoning of each side.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The argument is only about a dry לולב, and it depends on whether we compare the לולב to the אתרוג. A dry אתרוג is unfit according to everyone.

steps.title: Challenge: Why tie a spread-out לולב if beauty doesn't matter?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבא from a משנה where רבי יהודה says to tie a spread-out לולב from the top. That sounds like he cares about הדר.
steps.simpleTranslation: Does רבי יהודה really not require beauty for a לולב? But we learned in a משנה that רבי יהודה says to tie it at the top. Isn't the reason that he wants it to look beautiful?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רבא's explanation from Step 16. It uses another ruling of רבי יהודה that seems to show he does care about a nice-looking לולב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא said רבי יהודה does not compare a לולב to an אתרוג, so a לולב does not need הדר. But רבי יהודה says to tie together a לולב whose leaves spread out. Fixing the look of the לולב seems to be all about beauty.

keyTerms.meaning: Beauty: the requirement that the מצוה item look nice
Is it not because…? (a challenge that suggests a reason)

phrases.english: And with a lulav, does Rabbi Yehuda not require "beauty"?
But didn't we learn in a Mishnah: Rabbi Yehuda says:
He should tie it from the top.
What is the reason?
Is it not because he requires "beauty"?

steps.triggerLanguage: וּבְלוּלָב לָא בָּעֵי רַבִּי יְהוּדָה ״הָדָר״? וְהָתְנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבא's claim from Step 16 that רבי יהודה does not require הדר for a לולב.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's claim that רבי יהודה does not require הדר for a לולב
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Tying a spread-out לולב only makes sense as a way to make it look nice. So רבי יהודה must require הדר.

steps.title: Answer: Tying comes from the word כפות, not from beauty
steps.stepSummary: The tying rule comes from the פסוק's word כפות, which hints at 'tied'. It has nothing to do with הדר.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. The reason is taught: רבי יהודה says in the name of רבי טרפון that the פסוק says כפות תמרים. Read it as 'tied'. So if the leaves spread apart, tie them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. רבי יהודה gives his own reason for tying, and that reason is a word in the פסוק, not beauty.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word כַּפּוֹת sounds like כְּפוּת, meaning 'tied'. So the Torah's own description of a לולב is a closed, tied-together branch. This is a requirement about what a לולב is, not about how nice it looks, so רבא's claim stands.

keyTerms.meaning: Branches of date palms, the Torah's name for the לולב
As the reason is taught (the source itself gives the reason)

phrases.english: No, as the reason is taught:

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי טַרְפוֹן:
phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda says in the name of Rabbi Tarfon:
"Branches of date palms"
means "tied";
phrases.notes: A play on words: כַּפּוֹת (branches) is read like כְּפוּת (tied).

phrases.english: and if it was spread apart, he should tie it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in Step 17 by giving a different reason for tying.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Gives a different source: a reading of a word in the פסוק, not הדר
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought tying the לולב was about making it look beautiful.
steps.terutzMaskana: Tying comes from the word כפות. רבי יהודה still does not need הדר for a לולב.

steps.title: Second challenge: Why tie the לולב only with its own kind?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges again from רבי יהודה's rule that a לולב may be tied only with its own species. That also sounds like a concern for הדר.
steps.simpleTranslation: Does he really not require beauty? But we learned: you may tie a לולב only with its own kind, says רבי יהודה. Isn't the reason that he wants it to look beautiful?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second ruling of רבי יהודה to challenge רבא again.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Tying a לולב with palm material instead of string seems to be about keeping it looking nice and matching. If so, רבי יהודה does care about הדר for a לולב after all.

phrases.english: And does he not require "beauty"?
But didn't we learn: One does not tie the lulav
except with its own kind; these are the words of Rabbi Yehuda.
What is the reason?
Is it not because he requires "beauty"?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new challenge against רבא's claim from Step 16, after the first one was answered.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's claim that רבי יהודה does not require הדר for a לולב
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Insisting that the tie come from the same species looks like a concern for appearance, which means הדר.

steps.title: Answer: Even ugly palm parts are allowed for tying
steps.stepSummary: רבא says that even rough palm fiber or the palm's root may be used. These are not beautiful, so the rule cannot be about הדר.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. רבא said that you may tie it even with palm fiber, and even with the root of the palm tree.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the second challenge with a statement of רבא. It shows that 'its own kind' allows even unattractive materials.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If beauty were the reason, rough fiber or a root would not be allowed. Since they are allowed, the 'own kind' rule must have some other reason. That reason comes in the next steps.

keyTerms.meaning: Rough fiber that grows around the palm trunk
The root of the date palm

phrases.english: No, for Rava said:
even with palm fiber,
and even with the root of the date palm.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof in Step 19 by showing that unattractive materials are allowed.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Disproves the suggested reason by showing materials that are not beautiful are allowed
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought 'only its own kind' was a beauty rule.
steps.terutzMaskana: Ugly palm parts are allowed, so the rule is not about הדר.

steps.title: Then what is רבי יהודה's real reason?
steps.stepSummary: If beauty is not the reason, the גמרא asks why רבי יהודה requires tying with the same species.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, what is רבי יהודה's reason there?
steps.whatsHappening: This is a short setup question. The גמרא asks for the real reason, and the answer comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 20 showed what the reason is not. Now there is a gap, because the 'own kind' rule still needs an explanation.

keyTerms.meaning: But rather (if not that, then what?)

phrases.english: [But rather,] what is the reason
phrases.notes: Some versions add the word in square brackets. The question works either way.

phrases.english: of Rabbi Yehuda there?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאֶלָּא מַאי טַעְמָא דְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה הָתָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows from Step 20. Once beauty is ruled out, a new reason is needed.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The real reason רבי יהודה requires tying the לולב only with its own species.

steps.title: Because a different species would make five מינים
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה holds that the tie is part of the לולב. Tying with a different species would add a fifth species to the ארבעה מינים.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because he holds that a לולב needs to be tied. If you bring a different kind to tie it, you now have five species.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives רבי יהודה's real reason. It ends the challenge, and רבא's view stays in place.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי יהודה the tie is a required part of the מצוה. So the material of the tie counts as part of the bundle. Palm material stays part of the לולב, but a different plant would become a fifth species. The rule is about how many species there are, not about beauty.

keyTerms.meaning: Five species instead of the required four

steps.whatToRemember: Both rulings of רבי יהודה about tying have reasons other than beauty. Tying comes from the word כפות, and tying with its own kind avoids having חמשה מינין. So רבא's claim holds: for a לולב, רבי יהודה does not require הדר.
steps.confusionAlert: The 'own kind' rule is not about looks, because even rough fiber or a root is allowed. It is about the tie becoming part of the מצוה.

phrases.english: Because he holds that a lulav needs to be tied,
and if he brings a different species to tie it,
they become five species.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 21.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The tie is a required part of the לולב, so tying with a different species would turn the ארבעה מינים into five.

steps.title: Does רבי יהודה even require beauty for an אתרוג?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the idea that רבי יהודה requires הדר, quoting a ברייתא where he allows even a dry אתרוג.
steps.simpleTranslation: Does רבי יהודה really require beauty for an אתרוג? But a ברייתא teaches: You may not take fewer than the four species, and you may not add to them. If you cannot find an אתרוג, do not bring a quince, a pomegranate, or anything else instead. Slightly wilted species are כשר, and dry ones are פסול. רבי יהודה says: even dry ones are כשר.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks whether רבי יהודה cares about הדר for an אתרוג at all. It brings a ברייתא where he allows dry species, which are clearly not beautiful.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא said that for an אתרוג everyone agrees הדר is required, so a dry אתרוג should be פסול even for רבי יהודה. But in this ברייתא רבי יהודה allows dry species, and that includes the אתרוג. So it seems he does not require הדר even for an אתרוג, which contradicts רבא.

keyTerms.meaning: Beauty; the requirement that the species be nice-looking
One may not add (another species to the four)
A quince, a fruit that looks a bit like an אתרוג
Slightly wilted or partly dried out

steps.confusionAlert: The rule 'do not add' in this ברייתא is a different idea from הדר. The key point for the question is the very last line: רבי יהודה allows dry species.

phrases.aramaic: וּבְאֶתְרוֹג מִי בָּעֵי רַבִּי יְהוּדָה הָדָר?
phrases.english: And with an etrog, does Rabbi Yehuda require beauty?
But isn't it taught in a baraita: The four species of the lulav,
just as one may not take fewer than them
so too one may not add to them.
If one did not find an etrog,

phrases.aramaic: לֹא יָבִיא לֹא פָּרִישׁ וְלֹא רִמּוֹן
phrases.english: he should not bring a quince or a pomegranate
or anything else.
Slightly wilted ones are fit;
dry ones are unfit.
Rabbi Yehuda says: Even dry ones are fit.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּבְאֶתְרוֹג מִי בָּעֵי רַבִּי יְהוּדָה הָדָר? וְהָתַנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The לולב challenges to רבא are now answered. The גמרא turns to the other half of רבא's statement in Step 16, that everyone agrees an אתרוג needs הדר, and challenges it from a ברייתא where רבי יהודה allows dry species.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's statement in Step 16 that for an אתרוג everyone, including רבי יהודה, requires הדר (בְּאֶתְרוֹג — דִּבְרֵי הַכֹּל הָדָר בָּעֵינַן).
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי יהודה allows dry species in the ברייתא. A dry אתרוג is not beautiful, so it seems he does not require הדר.

steps.title: רבי יהודה begins telling a story
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues: רבי יהודה starts to bring a story that supports his view.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יהודה said: There was an incident...
steps.whatsHappening: This line is a setup. רבי יהודה is about to tell a story to support his view, and the story continues in the next lines.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is still part of the same ברייתא the גמרא is using to challenge. רבי יהודה backs up his ruling that dry species are fine with a real-life event.

keyTerms.meaning: A real event or story, often brought as proof for a halacha

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yehuda said: There was an incident

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא, with רבי יהודה starting to bring proof for allowing dry species.
steps.raayaObject: רבי יהודה's ruling that dry species are כשר.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A real-life incident that רבי יהודה reports. The details continue past this section.
